newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says this is testing time for Kabila.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says this is testing time for Kabila.

text.p: On the eve of what could be a make-or-break meeting for Zaire's political future, the United States on Tuesday pressed rebel leader Laurent Kabila to be a responsible leader and set markers on how he will be judged.
This is a "time of testing" for Kabila, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

Kabila "has enormous authority over one of the most important countries in Africa ... And we hope very much that he will be able to meet these tests," Burns said, adding: "We have very high standards."

Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and Kabila were scheduled to meet on Wednesday to discuss arrangements for a political transition in Zaire. If it does not go well, the rebel leader has warned his troops would take the capital Kinshasa by force.
Burns said Kabila needs to "protect the people who have come under his responsibility and here we're talking about the refugees."

He noted that the United Nations is investigating reports of widescale massacres of refugees at Kisangani. Asserting that "someone's going to have to answer for that," Burns said Kabila and his allies should be open to the probe by the United Nations special rapporteur.
The second test for Kabila will "be to see how he and the rebels comport themselves as they continue their march toward Kinshasa," Burns said.

"We believe very strongly it's in their interest, the rebel interest, as well as the interests of the people of the country to try to effect a peaceful entry of those forces into Kinshasa," the spokesman said.
This is expected to be discussed when Mobutu and Kabila meet on Wednesday under South African auspices.

Finally, Burns said, "another part of this testing for Mr. Kabila is whether or not, if he does gain power, he rules in a democratic fashion, both political and economically, and if he pays attention to the human rights of the people of Zaire."
Burns defended the decision to bring U.N. ambassador Bill Richardson, who was sent to Africa as a special U.S. envoy on the Zaire crisis, back to the United States.

Despite the uncertainty that still exists over the crucial end game in Zaire's civil war, Burns said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Richardson felt he had "accomplished the mission he set out to do" and was no longer needed in the region.
